entities.name: Aulus Plautius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aulus Plautius, a distinguished Roman senator and general, indelibly shaped the course of British history by initiating the full-scale Roman invasion of the island in 43 CE. As the architect of Emperor Claudius's ambitious campaign, Plautius commanded four legions and an equal number of auxiliaries, approximately 40,000 troops, establishing the foundational presence of Roman power that would endure for nearly four centuries. His decisive military actions and subsequent administrative tenure as the first governor of Britannia laid the groundwork for the province's integration into the Roman Empire, transforming a diverse collection of Celtic tribes into a frontier territory of Rome.

The invasion itself was a formidable undertaking, launched from Gaul and landing, most likely, near Richborough in Kent. Plautius's forces engaged and defeated the Catuvellauni and Trinovantes, prominent British tribes led by Caratacus and Togodumnus, in a series of critical battles, including the crossing of the Medway and Thames rivers. The capture of Camulodunum (modern Colchester), the capital of the Catuvellauni, marked a pivotal moment, leading to Claudius's personal, albeit brief, visit to Britain to celebrate the victory. Plautius's strategic genius secured a significant portion of southeastern Britain, creating a secure base from which future Roman expansion would proceed.
